newsitem.title: INDIA: India's falling exports cause grave concern-trade.
newsitem.headline: India's falling exports cause grave concern-trade.

text.p: A negative growth in India's exports at the start of 1997/98 (April/March) is causing grave concern among exporters, the head of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO) said on Thursday.
"It's a very serious situation and it's causing grave concern to exporters," FIEO president Ramu Deora told Reuters.
Deora said the rate of export growth in April 1997 was a negative 10.8 percent compared to 13.7 percent in the same month in the previous year. He did not give details.
The Economic Times newspaper, quoting official figures, said growth of Indian exports in the first quarter of fiscal 1997/98 could be a negative 5.0/6.0 percent.

Exporters said the current trend appeared to be a take-off from the previous year's poor performance. India's export growth in 1996/97 was a meagre 4.0 percent compared to 21.4 percent in the previous year.
Deora said all export goods, industrial and agricultural and other items like chemicals and gems and jewellery had been hit.
He said representatives of FIEO and various export promotion councils would meet the commerce minister in New Delhi on June 26 to discuss measures to reverse the fall in exports.
"We are going to discuss the recession in international markets and problems faced by exporters at home," Deora said.
He said the cost of export credit in India was as high as 13-18 percent against an average 9.0 percent in competing countries.
"The Indian exchange rate is unrealistic and unremunerative as far as exports are concerned," he said. "The Indian rupee should have been adjusted downwards by at least 10 percent to 38-40 rupees."
The Indian rupee has been steady at 35.75/85 against the dollar since mid-1996.
"Countries like Malaysia, Indonesia and Pakistan have devalued their currencies to boost exports. Why can't India do it?," Deora said.
He said many export houses were losing interest in their business due to unencouraging attitude of government agencies implementing export policies.
"Export business is fast becoming risky, unremunerative and unprofitable," Deora said.
Labour unrest in State Bank of India (SBI) and its branches in western India in the past one week hit exporters in the region who depened on credit from the bank.
SBI officers, who went on a week-long strike against suspension of three colleagues on charges of involvement in a financial scandal, on Thursday resumed work.
In April, a 10-day strike by truck operators brought foreign trade to a halt, causing severe losses to exporters.
